title: What patterns link digital roots, odd and even, and remainders?
description: We guess patterns from examples. Ten, eleven and twelve show that even or odd does not decide the digital root. The remainders on division by nine and by three then follow from the root, and a check with fourteen and twenty seven confirms them.
teaching_notes: One idea: a conjecture is a guess made from examples and then tested, and the digital root gives the remainder on division by nine. Watch for students who think an even number must have an even digital root.

video_script.why: A learner guesses patterns from examples between a number's parity, its digital root and its remainders on division by three and nine.
video_script.substitution: the book's own two questions, parity and remainders on division by 3 and 9
video_script.anchor: a table of the numbers 10, 11, 12 with their digital roots and remainders on division by 9
video_script.payoff_line: Even or odd does not decide the digital root. The root tells the remainder on division by nine and by three.

final_answer.value: (i) No fixed link between parity and digital root (ii) The digital root is the remainder on division by 9 (9 for remainder 0), and its remainder on division by 3 is the number's remainder on division by 3
final_answer.spoken: even or odd does not decide the digital root, and the root tells the remainder on division by nine and by three

hold_back: (i) No fixed link between parity and digital root (ii) The digital root is the remainder on division by 9 (9 for remainder 0), and its remainder on division by 3 is the number's remainder on division by 3
maths_rules: 10 is even with digital root 1 (odd); 11 is odd with digital root 2 (even); 12 is even with digital root 3 (odd); so parity does not decide the parity of the root
10, 11, 12 leave remainders 1, 2, 3 on division by 9, the same as their digital roots; a digital root of 9 means remainder 0
9 is a multiple of 3, so the remainder on division by 3 comes from the remainder on division by 9; digital roots 3, 6 and 9 give remainder 0
check 14: digital root 1 + 4 = 5, remainder 5 on division by 9 (14 = 9 + 5), remainder 2 on division by 3 (14 = 12 + 2) and 5 leaves 2 on division by 3
check 27: digital root 2 + 7 = 9, remainder 0 on division by 9 and by 3
video_script.design: One idea: guess patterns from examples, then test them with the digital root as a remainder on division by nine. Assumes the link between the digital root and the remainder on division by nine. The table of examples stays on the board all video.
